catalog_locator: thesis p. 57 (§3.3 Syllables); p. 95 (§4.6 The Tones of Makyam Naga (ST)); p. 137 (§6.2.1 Syllable and word structures); p. 146 (§6.2.5 A comparison of tones).
catalog_quote: [p. 57] Since Makyam Naga is a tonal language, every syllable of a Makyam word always has some type of tone which is abbreviated as (T) in many of the examples in this chapter. [p. 95] Makyam Naga is a tone language because use of different pitch can result in different meanings in Makyam Naga. ... The following examples are provided to prove that Makyam Naga is a tonal language. 1. to be good /tʃa²⁴ kɔ³¹/ ... 2. (be) honest /tʃa³³ kɔ³¹/ ... [p. 137] It is common to have 1‒3 syllables in a word in Makyam Naga. ... It is assumed that the longer multisyllabic words include affixes. However, it is difficult to determine whether multisyllabic utterances are single words or a phrase or a sentence since the meaning of each syllable of the word was not investigated. More investigation on the stem and intonation, clitic behaviour, deletion rules, minimal representations, and semantics, etc., is needed. [p. 146] The result of the analysis of the collected of the four LRPs from the two villages shows that Makyam Naga has five contrastive tones: two level tones and three contour tones.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given anywhere in the only descriptive phonology. Makyam Naga is described as a tone language in which every syllable of a word bears one of five lexical tones (Mid Level [33], High Level [44], Low/Mid-Rising [24]/[35], High-Falling [52]/[42], Low/Mid-Falling [21]/[31]); polysyllabic words are transcribed with a tone on each syllable and no syllable is marked as prominent or reduced.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone contours vary between speakers and villages (San Tong vs Kha Lai); tone sandhi in compounds is flagged as unstudied (p. 148).
new_statements.domain_note: Elicited isolated words from a 1,650-item wordlist (citation forms), two villages (San Tong, Kha Lai), Lahe Township, Sagaing Region, Myanmar; tone measured on monosyllabic open-syllable words; no connected speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Sawu 2016 describes 'Makyam Naga' (autonym Paung Nyuan; ISO umn) as spoken in San Tong and Kha Lai villages, Lahe Township, Naga Self-Administered Zone, Sagaing Region, Myanmar, i.e. the same languoid as Glottolog maky1235 (Glottolog 5.1 'Makyam-Kuku Naga', 5.3 'Makyamic', alt. 'Makyan Naga'). Sawu (following Wayesha, Sein Maung & Mann 2007) places it in Khiamniungic (Leinong-Makyam), while the abstract also cites the older Konyak-Bodo-Garo/Northern Naga placement; no dialect other than the two village varieties is treated.

sources.note: Silent on word stress: the word 'stress' occurs only inside a quoted Crystal (2008) definition of 'contour tone' (glossary and p. 37); no section on stress, accent or prominence. States Makyam Naga is a tone language with five contrastive tones (two level, three contour) and that every syllable of a word carries a tone (syllable formula CV(V)(C)T), pp. iii, 57, 95, 146-147. Tone analysed only on isolated monosyllables; tone sandhi left for future work (p. 148).
